trainings.restrictions: F4: proposed; no specific training source (source null). Prefer images or authorised points; do not extrapolate Earth wind directly to Mars or disturb dunes and wetlands.

tata-sabaya.name: Tata Sabaya volcano, Oruro, Bolivia
tata-sabaya.why: About 12,000 years ago its flank collapsed and formed a debris avalanche that left mounds, now "islands" in the Coipasa salt flat. It is an analog of volcanic collapses and of the large landslides of Mars. Support: suggested.
tata-sabaya.breakingPoint: Its collapse, about 12,000 years ago, happened on a small Andean volcano. The large landslides of Valles Marineris and the flanks of Olympus Mons are on a much larger scale.

geomorphological.covers: Debris avalanche of about 6 km³ that covered 230–300 km² and left mounds, like the large landslides of Mars.
geomorphological.breaks: The landslides of Valles Marineris travel tens of kilometres and the flanks of Olympus Mons are much larger. Earth's gravity changes how an avalanche moves.

trainings.activity: Proposal: map the mounds and edges of the avalanche deposit on an elevation model and test hypotheses of slope movement.
trainings.measures: Area outlined, dimensions with uncertainty and agreement with the deposit described in the study.
trainings.restrictions: F4: suggested as an analog; the study supports the Earth geology. Do not equate scale and gravity with Mars. Use remote data before any authorised campaign.

tolbachik.name: Tolbachik volcano, Kamchatka, Russia
tolbachik.why: Active volcanic complex with cinder cones, lava fields, lava tubes and permafrost inside volcanic deposits. Its cones have been compared with possible volcanic cones in northern Mars and its scoria has a texture close to that of Martian regolith. Coordinates of its permafrost monitoring station. UNESCO World Heritage site: permits required.
tolbachik.breakingPoint: It is an active volcano, with up to 2 m of snow and permafrost around 0 °C at 1,100 m altitude. The volcanoes of Tharsis went extinct long ago and Martian ground is far below 0 °C, in 0.38 times Earth's gravity.

geomorphological.covers: The 1975–76 eruption covered about 500 km² with scoria and ash and formed three new cones and lava fields; its cones have been compared with 14 possible volcanic cones in northern Mars. It has lava tubes, the most likely type of cave on Mars, and ash-covered glaciers studied as an analog of Martian glaciers.
geomorphological.breaks: These are recent cones and flows, small compared with Tharsis, and the comparison is one of shape: it does not confirm that those Martian cones are volcanic. Its largest cave, Shokoladnaya, is 339 m long; Martian tubes are thought to be much larger.

mineralogical.covers: Highly porous basaltic scoria, with a texture close to that of Martian regolith and very low thermal conductivity: 0.17 W/m·K dry and 0.44 W/m·K at 45 % moisture.
mineralogical.breaks: The tubes from the 2012–13 eruption contain unusual mineral formations, but without quantitative data. The scoria is similar in texture; these sources have not compared its composition with that of Martian regolith.

environmental.covers: Permafrost inside scoria and ash: a frozen layer 12 to 16 m thick, with mean temperatures of 0 to −1 °C at 1,100 m and about −7 °C at 2,600 m. Viable microbes and methane were found in this volcanic permafrost (about 1,100–1,900 µl of CH₄ per kg of sample).
environmental.breaks: It is warm permafrost, close to 0 °C, with more than 2 m of snow in forested areas and dense air; the ground on Mars is far below zero. No data on light or dust: there is no polar night and no dust storms, only ash falling on the snow.

trainings.activity: Monitor permafrost inside volcanic deposits with boreholes and temperature loggers, as at its station at 1,330 m.
trainings.measures: Ground temperature at different depths and altitudes (loggers between 800 and 3,075 m) and active-layer thickness.
trainings.restrictions: UNESCO World Heritage site and protected area: access requires permits.

trainings.activity: Practise 3D mapping of lava tubes and volcanic caves, like the topographic model of the Luch-2 tube.
trainings.measures: Accuracy of the 3D model and of the traverse; for reference, Shokoladnaya cave is 339 m long and 25 m deep.
trainings.restrictions: Active volcano and protected area: access with permits.

trainings.activity: Measure the thermal properties of the scoria, whose texture is similar to that of Martian regolith.
trainings.measures: Thermal conductivity depending on moisture: 0.17 W/m·K dry and 0.44 W/m·K at 45 % moisture.

torotoro.name: Torotoro National Park, Bolivia
torotoro.why: Canyon 250–300 m deep with exposed sedimentary layers, for training in reading strata and interpreting images, as rover teams do. An analogy of method: its origin is fluvial, not tectonic like Valles Marineris. Support: suggested.
torotoro.breakingPoint: It is useful for training in reading layers, but its canyon is fluvial and about 300 m deep. Valles Marineris is tectonic and reaches 7 km in depth.

geomorphological.covers: Canyon 250–300 m deep with layers of shale, sandstone and limestone, and a large fold (syncline).
geomorphological.breaks: Its origin is fluvial and its scale small: Valles Marineris is tectonic and reaches about 7 km in depth. The rocks of Gale have a different age and composition.

operational.covers: Training in reading strata: identifying layers and contacts and photographing them with a scale, as rover teams do.
operational.breaks: It is an analogy of method, not of rocks. The protection of its fossil footprints limits physical work and sampling.

trainings.activity: F2 proposal: describe contacts between layers with photographs and send an interpretation to the remote team within an allotted time.
trainings.measures: Contacts recognised, complete reports, decision time and agreement with a specialist-reviewed reference.
trainings.restrictions: F4: suggested; F2, section 4.6. No specific source for carrying it out (source null). Strict protection of fossils and formations; no extraction and no leaving authorised trails.

trainings.activity: F2 proposal: evaluate strata segmentation and route planning on photographs or a validated digital model.
trainings.measures: Strata precision and recall, map error, simulated collisions and routes completed.
trainings.restrictions: F2, section 4.6; no specific source for the exercise (source null). Do not drive over heritage sites. A visual model does not prove real climbing ability or geological equivalence with Mars.

umajalanta.name: Umajalanta Cave, Torotoro, Bolivia
umajalanta.why: The longest cave in Bolivia (about 4.6 km). It is used to practise underground navigation, communications and mapping. It is a limestone cave, not a lava tube: the analog is operational, not geological. Support: suggested.
umajalanta.breakingPoint: It is a limestone cave dissolved by water, not a lava tube. It is useful for practising underground navigation and communications, not for studying the geology of Marius Hills.

operational.covers: Underground navigation, communications and mapping in a cave about 4.6 km long.
operational.breaks: Its passages are narrow, wet and have an underground river; a lunar tube would be dry, airless and perhaps much wider. Equipment and routes tested here must be adapted to those differences. For practising in real lava tubes there are volcanic analogs such as Tolbachik, in Kamchatka.

trainings.activity: Proposal: evaluate navigation without GNSS and mapping of underground passages on a digital model or replica of the cave.
trainings.measures: Map error, tracking losses, coverage, link recovery and simulated collisions.
trainings.restrictions: F4: suggested; no specific source for the exercise (source null). Prioritise models; fieldwork only with authorisation and specialists. A limestone cave does not reproduce a lunar lava tube.

uyuni.name: Salar de Uyuni, Bolivia
uyuni.why: A single salt flat that supports several comparisons with Mars. Its salt crusts, brines and clays resemble Aureum Chaos (proposed by NASA), and its chlorides have been compared with those of Icaria Planum (UMSA, EPSC 2024). Its lithium- and magnesium-rich brines host salt-adapted microbes (studied). Its natural salt polygons, 1–2 m across, form by brine convection, not by ice (Physical Review X, 2023). Its flat, repetitive surface is useful for testing rover navigation (proposal from the F2 report). No perchlorates are attributed to it without local analysis.
uyuni.breakingPoint: It floods with rainwater every year at Earth pressure and its salt is recent: Aureum Chaos and Icaria Planum have been dry and frozen for billions of years. Its brines are abundant and mild; those of Mars, if they exist, would be scarce, temporary and very cold. Its polygons come from the brine, not from ice, and no perchlorates are attributed to it without local analysis.

geomorphological.covers: Natural polygons 1–2 m across in the crust, formed by brine convection beneath the surface: a counterexample of polygons without ice.
geomorphological.breaks: It does not represent the ice polygons of Utopia Planitia. It is useful for not confusing causes, especially in salt deposits such as those of Icaria Planum. The polygonal salt crusts of Qaidam (China) allow comparing the same phenomenon in another salt flat.

mineralogical.covers: Salt crusts, brines and hydrated clays that NASA compares with Aureum Chaos, and chlorides formed by evaporation that UMSA researchers compared with those of Icaria Planum. Its brines contain chlorides and lithium and magnesium salts.
mineralogical.breaks: No perchlorates are attributed to it without local analysis, and its salt is recent: the deposits of Aureum Chaos, Icaria Planum and Meridiani are billions of years old. The chlorides of Icaria Planum are detected from orbit, so the comparison depends on what those instruments can see. Perchlorates have been detected in the soil of Dalangtan (Qaidam, China).

environmental.covers: Night-time cold, dry air and high UV radiation over a salt surface. Its lithium- and magnesium-rich brines contain salts that destabilise biomolecules and still host microbes even 80 m deep.
environmental.breaks: There is oxygen, pressure is tens of times that of Mars and it floods with rainwater every year. Its microbes grow at Earth temperature and pressure; to know whether they would survive on Mars they would need to be exposed in the laboratory to extreme cold, low pressure and radiation. For Mars, −25 °C or above and water activity greater than 0.5 are used as reference; those values would need to be measured at Uyuni.

operational.covers: Flat, repetitive surface for testing a rover's visual localisation, mapping and crust detection.
operational.breaks: Meridiani has sand ripples and spherules. The crust can hide brine or soft areas, and salt corrodes contacts and equipment.

trainings.activity: F2 proposal: plan non-invasive observations of deposits and crusts within a time budget, with remote science support.
trainings.measures: Targets completed, quality of photographs and records, return time and risks correctly identified.
trainings.restrictions: F4: proposed by NASA for the site; F2, section 4.1. No specific source for the exercise (source null). Authorised sectors and an assessed crust; do not drill or assume uniform firmness.

trainings.activity: F2 proposal: evaluate changes in test specimens of covers and connectors exposed to the salty environment, comparing them with protected controls.
trainings.measures: Salt deposited, change in transmittance, contact resistance and damage after a defined cleaning.
trainings.restrictions: F2, sections 4.1 and 8; no specific campaign source (source null). Retrievable specimens, without releasing materials or soiling the salt flat. It is not equivalent to abrasion by lunar dust and does not certify a suit.

trainings.activity: Proposal: reproduce a cartographic comparison of chlorides using orbital images and explain the similarities and differences between Uyuni and Icaria Planum.
trainings.measures: Deposit boundaries, agreement between observers, resolution uncertainty and spectral evidence for each classification.
trainings.restrictions: The conference abstract supports the comparison, not a full identity. Do not infer perchlorates or life; use the original coordinates and data, without carrying over unverified figures.

trainings.activity: F2 proposal: drive an inspected route using a camera and IMU, keeping GNSS as an external evaluation reference.
trainings.measures: Lateral and final error, drift per distance, tracking losses and energy per metre.
trainings.restrictions: F2, section 4.1; no specific source for a completed test (source null). Do not degrade safety communications; check the crust, light and humidity. Do not drive through water or uncertain sectors.

trainings.activity: F2 proposal: classify images of crusts and evaluate whether the system recognises uncertainty and asks to stop before moving on.
trainings.measures: False negatives for unsafe ground, false alarms, stopping time and correct requests for help.
trainings.restrictions: F2, sections 4.1 and 8; no specific source for the exercise (source null). Use a labelled dataset or a replica track; do not check errors by driving towards dangerous crusts.

trainings.activity: Proposal: measure the size and spacing of polygons in images and weigh explanations by brine, ice or contraction without deciding from shape alone.
trainings.measures: Size distribution, scale uncertainty and the independent evidence needed for each hypothesis.
trainings.restrictions: F4: studied for the salt-polygon mechanism. The study does not show the cause of each local polygon or of the Martian ones. Do not dig trenches or disturb crusts.

trainings.activity: Proposal: practise recording, blanks and traceability for a brine study using artificial samples of known composition.
trainings.measures: Labelling errors, contaminated blanks, recovery of known components and complete records.
trainings.restrictions: F4: studied for the site; method from F2, section 4.7. No specific source for the exercise (source null). Do not attribute perchlorates to Uyuni or present-day water to RSL; no unauthorised extraction.

valle-de-la-luna.name: Valle de la Luna, Mallasa, La Paz, Bolivia
valle-de-la-luna.why: Gullies, pinnacles and shadows for practising photogrammetry, 3D mapping and rover navigation. Digital models are recommended: the formations are fragile. Similar relief does not imply the same origin. Support: methodological candidate (F2).
valle-de-la-luna.breakingPoint: It is useful for practising 3D mapping, but its relief was shaped by rain on soft clays. Gale has no rain today and its relief is much older.

geomorphological.covers: Relief eroded into gullies and pinnacles in soft sediments.
geomorphological.breaks: Its pinnacles are a few metres tall and fragile; the landforms of Gale are made of harder, older rock. It is useful for practising how relief looks, not for understanding how it formed.

operational.covers: Gullies, pinnacles and shadows for practising photogrammetry, 3D mapping and obstacle detection.
operational.breaks: The formations are fragile: digital models or replicas are advisable. It does not reproduce the light, dust or gravity of Mars.

trainings.activity: F2 proposal: build a digital model from authorised photographs and test edge detection and routes between gullies.
trainings.measures: Reconstruction error, obstacles missed, false detections caused by shadows and virtual routes completed.
trainings.restrictions: F2, section 4.5: methodological candidate with no specific source for carrying it out (source null). Do not use the original formations as a track; work with digital twins or replicas.

trainings.activity: F2 proposal: interpret slopes and erosional landforms from images and explain which observations allow telling geological processes apart.
trainings.measures: Risks recognised, quality of hypotheses, photographic references and reporting time.
trainings.restrictions: F2, section 4.5; no specific source for the exercise (source null). Only permitted trails and observations; the site's name does not imply lunar geology.

yakutia.name: Central Yakutia, Lena River basin, Russia
yakutia.why: Very ice-rich permafrost, with thermokarst, thaw lakes and ice wedges. Its depressions along the banks of the Lena are compared with the scalloped depressions left by the sublimation of subsurface ice in Utopia Planitia. Approximate location (Yakutsk).
yakutia.breakingPoint: Its depressions form when ice melts and the water escapes; in Utopia Planitia the ice sublimates, turning straight into gas. In addition, in summer Yakutia reaches about 38 °C and has rivers with unfrozen ground beneath them.

geomorphological.covers: Thermokarst (ground subsiding as it loses ice) across about half of Yakutia, with lakes, ice wedges and depressions along the Lena compared with the scalloped depressions of Utopia Planitia.
geomorphological.breaks: In Yakutia the depressions form by thawing, with liquid water; in Utopia, by sublimation: the shape is similar, not the process. Beneath its rivers there are taliks, unfrozen ground, something not known in Utopia Planitia. No mineral data.

environmental.covers: One of the coldest inhabited places on Earth: a record −67.7 °C near Oymyakon and continuous permafrost at −5 to −13 °C. Siberian permafrost is about 350 m thick on average (up to 1,450 m) and up to 50 % ice between the grains; in northeastern Siberia it has been frozen for more than 3 million years.
environmental.breaks: In summer it reaches about 38 °C (a swing of more than 100 °C over the year) and the ground thaws down to 1.5–4 m; Mars is cold all year round, with a pressure of a few hundred pascals. No documented analog for dust.

trainings.activity: Compare the thermokarst and the depressions along the Lena with images of the scalloped depressions of Utopia Planitia.
trainings.measures: Shape, size and orientation of the depressions and ice content of the ground.
trainings.restrictions: They form by thawing, not by sublimation: the shape is compared, not the process.

trainings.activity: Study how very ice-rich permafrost responds to temperature changes.
trainings.measures: Permafrost temperature (−5 to −13 °C), active-layer thickness (1.5–4 m) and air warming trend (0.03 °C per year).
